name: Savings Groups and Microfinance (Chamas, VSLAs, Tontines, Esusu)

Given a goal and your own income, write a monthly savings plan with the goal, the total, the date, the amount per week or month and where you will save it, with arithmetic that adds up to the goal by the date

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Two kinds of savings groups
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how a rotating group and a saving-and-lending group work, and choose one for your goal.
This lesson builds toward: Given a savings goal and two kinds of group, you will explain how a rotating group and a saving-and-lending group work and choose the one that fits the goal, giving one reason for the choice and one risk of each.
A rotating group (a merry-go-round, esusu, ajo, susu, tontine, njangi, gam'eya or daret) is simple. Every member pays the same amount each week or month, and each time one member takes the whole pot, in turn, until everyone has had it once. Example: 10 members each pay KES 1,000 a month; each month one member gets KES 10,000.
It is good for a lump sum: school fees, a sewing machine, stock for a shop. Its risks: people who get the pot early may stop paying, and nobody earns anything on the money. Early members get an interest-free advance; late members are really lending to the group.
A saving-and-lending group (a VSLA, an ASCA or many chamas, and in a bigger, formal version a SACCO) keeps the money together. Members save at each meeting, the savings become a loan fund, members borrow and repay with a service charge the group sets, and at the end of the cycle, often about a year, everything is shared out in proportion to what each member saved. Its risks: loans that are not repaid, and cash that is stolen or badly recorded.
Choose by your goal. A lump sum soon: a rotating group may fit. Steady saving with the chance to borrow: a saving-and-lending group may fit. Many people use both.
Words to know:
- Rotating group (ROSCA): members pay the same amount and each takes the whole pot in turn.
- Saving-and-lending group: members save into a shared fund, lend to each other and share out at the end of a cycle (VSLA, ASCA, SACCO).
- Share-out: the day a group pays out all savings and earnings to members in proportion to their savings.
Official sources:
- VSL Associates: the VSLA methodology (shares, loan fund, social fund, one-year cycle, share-out)
Try it now: Think of a group you are in or know. Is it rotating or saving-and-lending? Write one thing it is good for and one risk.
You can now explain the two kinds of savings groups and choose the one that fits your goal.

check.q: Twelve members each pay GHS 200 a month and one member takes the whole pot each month. What kind of group is this?
check.why: Everyone pays the same and takes the pot in turn: a rotating group (susu).

check.q: In a VSLA, how is money shared out at the end of the cycle?
options: In proportion to what each member saved
check.why: Members who saved more get a bigger share of the fund and its earnings.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Your goal and monthly savings plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a savings plan that reaches a goal by a date.
This lesson builds toward: Given a goal and your own income, you will write a monthly savings plan with the goal, the total, the date, the amount per week or month and where you will save it, with arithmetic that adds up to the goal by the date.
Saving works better with a clear goal: what it is for, how much it costs and when you need it. "School fees of NGN 120,000 by January" is a goal. "Save more" is not.
Divide the total by the number of weeks or months you have. Example: NGN 120,000 in 8 months is NGN 15,000 a month. If that is too much, change the date, the goal or your spending. Look at your income on good and bad months; a trader may save more in the busy season.
Decide where the money will sit: a savings group, a SACCO, a microfinance bank, a bank or a mobile savings account. Keep a small emergency amount you can reach quickly, separate from money for the goal.
Pay yourself first: save on the day money comes in, before other spending. Example: Aïcha, a hairdresser in Abidjan, puts XOF 5,000 in her tontine every Saturday before she buys anything else.
Step by step:
- Write the goal, the total and the date.
- Count the weeks or months until the date.
- Divide the total by that number.
- Check it against your income on a bad month.
- Choose where to save it.
- Save on the day money comes in.
Words to know:
- Savings goal: what you save for, how much it costs and by when.
- Emergency money: a small amount kept aside for sudden problems, easy to reach.
Try it now: Write one real goal with a total and a date. Divide to get the amount per week or month, and check it against your income in a bad month. Change it until it works.
You can now write a savings plan with a goal, a total, a date and an amount per week or month.

check.q: You need KES 24,000 in 6 months. How much do you save each month?
Which is a clear savings goal?
options: "A sewing machine costing GHS 1,500 by June"
check.why: It says what, how much and by when.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Checking a group's rules before you join
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a group's written rules for the seven key points.
This lesson builds toward: Given a group's constitution or rules, you will check it for the key rules: contributions, meetings, loans, fines, leaving, share-out and who controls the money, finding at least six of the seven and naming any that are missing.
A strong group has written rules, often called a constitution or by-laws, agreed by all members. Ask to see them before you join. If there are none, ask the group to write them first.
Check seven things: 1. Contributions: how much, how often, and what happens if you pay late (fines). 2. Meetings: when and where. 3. Loans: who can borrow, how much, for how long, the service charge and what happens if a loan is not repaid. 4. Fines and discipline. 5. Leaving: how you get your money back if you leave or move. 6. Share-out or rotation order: when and how. 7. Who controls the money: the officers, how they are elected, and who signs.
Some groups register, for example as a self-help group, a cooperative or a SACCO; ask the local social development or cooperative office what applies where you live. A group that takes deposits from the public as a business may need a licence from the regulator.
Example: Grace's chama in Nakuru writes in its rules that the treasurer cannot also hold the cash box keys, and members vote on every loan.
Step by step:
- Ask to see the written rules.
- Check contributions and late fines.
- Check meeting days.
- Check loan rules and what happens if a loan is not repaid.
- Check how you leave and get your money back.
- Check share-out or rotation order.
- Check who controls and signs for the money.
Words to know:
- Constitution (by-laws): the written rules a group agrees and follows.
- Officers: members elected to lead: often a chair, a secretary and a treasurer.
Official sources:
- SASRA, Kenya: list of licensed deposit-taking SACCOs
- BCEAO: rules for microfinance institutions (systèmes financiers décentralisés) in XOF countries
Try it now: Get the rules of a group you are in or want to join (or write down what you know). Tick each of the seven points. Write the ones that are missing as questions to ask at the next meeting.
You can now check a group's rules for the seven key points before you trust it with your money.

options: What colour is the cash box?
If I move to another town, how do I get my savings back?
check.why: The leaving rule says how a member gets their money back.

check.q: A group has no written rules. What is a wise step before you join?
options: Ask the members to agree and write rules first
Join and hope for the best
Give your savings to the chair to keep
Join two groups to be safe
check.why: Written rules prevent most disputes about money.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Records, loans and staying safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Records and cash safety at meetings
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Record contributions and loans and check that the cash matches the records.
This lesson builds toward: At a group meeting, you will record contributions and loans in a passbook or record book and check that the cash and the records match, with every amount read out and agreed in front of members.
Most group failures start with poor records or one person holding the money. Good groups keep records that every member can follow.
Common tools: each member has a passbook showing their savings and loans, the group keeps a record book, and in many VSLAs the cash box has three locks with three keys held by three different members who are not the box keeper. Some groups keep money in a group bank or mobile account that needs two or three signatories.
At each meeting: every contribution and repayment is counted in front of members, written in the passbook and the record book, and the total is read out. At the end, the cash counted must match the records. If it does not, stop and find out why before anyone leaves.
Example: in a VSLA in Tamale, the secretary reads the balance aloud and two members count the cash. They match: GHS 3,450. The box is locked and the keys go home with three different members.
Step by step:
- Count each payment in front of members.
- Write it in the member's passbook and the record book.
- Read the totals aloud.
- Count the cash and compare with the record book.
- If they do not match, find out why before anyone leaves.
- Lock the cash; keys or signing power with different members.
Words to know:
- Passbook: a member's own book showing their savings and loans.
- Signatory: a person allowed to sign for the group's account; good groups need two or more.
Official sources:
- VSL Associates: the VSLA methodology (shares, loan fund, social fund, one-year cycle, share-out)
Try it now: Make a simple record table for one meeting: member name, savings paid, loan repaid, new loan. Add three example members. Total each column and check that the totals equal the cash you would count.
You can now record contributions and loans at a meeting and check that the cash matches the records.

check.q: At the end of a meeting, the cash is GHS 200 less than the record book. What do you do?
options: Ignore it; it will balance next time
Let the treasurer explain it next month
Stop and find out why before anyone leaves
check.why: A difference must be found while everyone is present and memories are fresh.

check.q: Why do many VSLAs give the three keys to three different members?
options: So no single person can open the box alone
So the box keeper can open it at home
check.why: Shared keys mean the cash can only be opened with members present.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Microfinance and group loans
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the total you will repay on a loan and check the dates against your income.
This lesson builds toward: Given a microfinance or group loan offer, you will calculate the total you will repay and check the repayment dates against your income, before you sign, and naming what joint liability means for you.
Microfinance banks and institutions lend smaller amounts to people and small businesses, often through groups. In Nigeria, the Central Bank licenses microfinance banks; in Kenya, the Central Bank licenses microfinance banks and digital credit providers; in Ghana, the Bank of Ghana lists licensed institutions; in XOF countries such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire, microfinance follows BCEAO rules.
Never compare loans only by the interest rate they say. Ask for the total you will repay, in writing, including all fees, insurance and charges. Example (made-up figures): borrow KES 10,000; repay KES 1,000 a week for 12 weeks. Total repaid: KES 12,000, so the loan costs KES 2,000.
Check the repayment dates against your income. A weekly repayment is hard if you earn monthly or seasonally. Ask what happens if you pay late: fines, and whether it is reported to a credit bureau.
Many group loans use joint liability: if one member does not pay, the others must pay for them. Join only with people you trust, and know that you may have to cover someone else. Borrow for something that earns or saves money, not to pay another loan.
Step by step:
- Ask for the total to be repaid, in writing, with all fees.
- Work out the cost: total repaid minus the amount borrowed.
- Write down the repayment dates.
- Check each date against your income in a bad month.
- Ask about late fines and credit reporting.
- Ask whether the loan has joint liability.
Words to know:
- Microfinance: small loans and savings services for people and small businesses.
- Total repaid: all the money you pay back, including interest and fees.
- Joint liability: group members must pay for a member who does not repay.
- Credit bureau: a company that records how people repay loans; lenders check it.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Nigeria: microfinance banks
- Central Bank of Kenya: bank supervision, including licensed microfinance banks and digital credit providers
- Bank of Ghana: all licensed institutions and complaints procedures
- BCEAO: rules for microfinance institutions (systèmes financiers décentralisés) in XOF countries
Try it now: Use this example or a real offer: borrow NGN 50,000 and repay NGN 4,800 a week for 12 weeks. Work out the total repaid and the cost. Then write whether weekly payments fit your income.
You can now work out the total you will repay on a loan and check that the dates fit your income before you sign.

check.q: You borrow GHS 1,000 and repay GHS 120 a month for 10 months. What is the total repaid?
In a group loan with joint liability, one member stops paying. What may happen?
options: The other members must pay for that member
check.why: Joint liability means members cover each other's unpaid loans.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Ponzi schemes, fake lenders and your plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the warning signs of a Ponzi scheme or fake lender and check a provider on the regulator's list.
This lesson builds toward: Given an offer to save, invest or borrow, you will identify the warning signs of a Ponzi scheme or fake lender and check the provider on the regulator's official list, before you pay or share any details. Given a goal and your own income, you will write a monthly savings plan with the goal, the total, the date, the amount per week or month and where you will save it, with arithmetic that adds up to the goal by the date.
A Ponzi scheme pays early members with new members' money. It always collapses, and most people lose their savings. Warning signs: promises to double your money or guaranteed high returns in a short time, pressure to recruit friends and family, rewards for recruiting, a business nobody can explain, and promotion through WhatsApp, TikTok, Instagram or Telegram groups and influencers. Nigeria's SEC has warned about such schemes many times.
Fake lenders and loan apps: they ask for a fee before giving the loan, ask for your PIN or password, demand access to all your phone contacts, or threaten and shame borrowers. Real lenders never need your PIN.
Check before you pay or share details. Look up the provider on the regulator's official list: SASRA for deposit-taking SACCOs and the Central Bank of Kenya for microfinance banks and digital lenders in Kenya; the CBN for microfinance banks and the FCCPC list of approved digital lenders in Nigeria; the Bank of Ghana's list of licensed institutions; the BCEAO and national ministries of finance in XOF countries. If it is not on the list, do not use it.
Then finish your plan: goal, total, date, amount per week or month, where you save, and your check-sheet answers about the group or institution.
Step by step:
- Ask: does it promise guaranteed or very high returns fast?
- Ask: does it pay me to recruit others?
- Ask: does it want a fee first, or my PIN?
- Look it up on the regulator's official list.
- Not on the list, or any warning sign: do not pay.
- Write your monthly savings plan and check sheet.
Words to know:
- Ponzi scheme: a fraud that pays old members with new members' money until it collapses.
- Regulator: the official body that licenses and supervises financial providers, such as a central bank.
- Licensed: officially allowed by the regulator to do this business.
Official sources:
- Nairametrics (14 May 2026): SEC Nigeria warns against Ponzi schemes promoted on WhatsApp, TikTok and Instagram
- SASRA, Kenya: list of licensed deposit-taking SACCOs
- Central Bank of Kenya: bank supervision, including licensed microfinance banks and digital credit providers
- FCCPC, Nigeria: registration status of digital money lenders (approved loan apps)
- Bank of Ghana: all licensed institutions and complaints procedures
- BCEAO: rules for microfinance institutions (systèmes financiers décentralisés) in XOF countries
Try it now: Final task: write your monthly savings plan with goal, total, date, amount per week or month and where you will save it. Add the check sheet: the group's rules, how cash and records are kept, the licence (checked on the regulator's list if needed) and any loan's total cost.
You can now spot a Ponzi scheme or fake lender, check a provider on the official list, and follow your written savings plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear goal and sum No total or date, or the amount per month does not add up to the goal. Goal, total, date and amount per week or month, with arithmetic that adds up. Also checked against a bad month's income and keeps emergency money separate. Right kind of saving No place to save chosen, or no reason. Names where the money will be saved and gives one reason it fits the goal and one risk. Compares two options (for example a rotating group and a SACCO) before choosing. Group rules checked Rules not seen or fewer than four of the seven points checked. At least six of the seven rule points checked, with missing ones listed as questions. All seven checked and the missing rules raised with the group. Records and cash safety Does not say how cash and records are kept. Says how cash is kept (three-lock box or account with two or more signatories) and that totals are read aloud. Includes a sample record table that balances. Loan cost and safety A loan is planned without the total repaid. Any loan has the total repaid, the cost and dates checked against income; or the plan has no loan. Also notes late fines, credit reporting and joint liability. Licence and scam check An unlicensed provider or a scheme with warning signs is in the plan. Any institution that takes deposits or lends as a business was checked on the regulator's official list, and no warning signs are present. Names the list used and the date checked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A WhatsApp group promises to double your money in 30 days and pays you for each friend you bring. What is it?
options: The signs of a Ponzi scheme
check.why: Fast guaranteed returns and recruiting rewards are classic Ponzi signs.

check.q: A loan app asks for a "processing fee" before it sends the loan. What do you do?
options: Do not pay; check it on the regulator's list
Pay quickly before the offer ends
check.why: A fee before the loan is a fake-lender sign; check the official list first.
